paras: The attempted lynching at Clarendon, Arkansas, was a mob's effort on the night of December 3, 1903, to lynch an unnamed Black prisoner who was on trial in the town. The sheriff protected the prisoner, and the only report of the mob said it was expected to return the following night.

Clarendon held prisoners from the surrounding area to await trial at the next term of the circuit court. In early November two Black youths, Norman Couch and Henry Bell, aged 14 and 19, were brought there under guard after being charged with killing Winnie Gideon at a gin house near Brinkley and hiding his body under cotton. Bell, named John Bell in later dispatches, came to trial there in December, though no account ties him to the mob.

According to the Newport Daily Independent of December 4, travelers arriving over the Choctaw railroad said that "a mob gathered in Clarendon last night, seeking to lynch a negro on trial there." The sheriff "was kept busy protecting his prisoner," the item continued, and it was thought the mob would come back that night, "so deeply are they bent upon lynching the negro." The report gave no name, charge, size of the mob or details of what the crowd did.

No later report of the mob's return, of arrests or of any official response was found. From Tuesday to Thursday of the following week, December 8 to 10, John Bell was tried at Clarendon for the murder of Winnie Gideon, described as a white boy of 12, and the jury returned a verdict of first-degree murder in under an hour. The case rested on the testimony of Couch, called an alleged accessory, who said Bell struck the boy with a stick after a quarrel over a pencil.

Sheriff Milwee hanged Bell at Clarendon on January 28, 1904, and Bell "protested his innocence to the very last." None of the trial or execution dispatches mentions a mob, so whether Bell was the prisoner the crowd sought cannot be settled from the coverage, and the mob gathered five days before his trial opened.

The mob appears in a single paragraph in the Newport Daily Independent, set among social notes and an insurance advertisement and attributed only to travelers' word. The item called the prisoner "a negro" and passed no judgment on the mob or the sheriff. The Bell case drew wider Arkansas coverage, with the trial dispatch carried by the Newport and Pine Bluff dailies and a brief headed "Brutal Murderer Convicted" in the Newport and Forrest City weeklies. His execution ran under "Negro Hanged at Clarendon" in both dailies on January 29, 1904.
No Black-press account of the mob or of the Bell case was found.

bases: A mob gathered to lynch a Black prisoner held by the sheriff at Clarendon and was held off, an attempted lynching (A2).

One short local item in the Newport daily independent, based on travelers' word, reports the mob; no other paper found mentions it (A2).

accounts.label: Travelers' report
accounts.gist: Arrivals over the Choctaw railroad said a mob gathered at Clarendon to lynch a Black prisoner on trial, that the sheriff protected him, and that the mob was expected back.

framing.detail: A one-paragraph local item amid social notes, calling the prisoner 'a negro' and the mob 'deeply... bent upon lynching', with no comment on either.
Coverage of the Bell case called him a 'Brutal Murderer' and the killing 'brutal' and did not mention any mob.

versions.value: Mob gathered the night of Dec. 3 against a prisoner 'on trial'

conflicts.note: If the prisoner was Bell, the mob came before his trial opened; the item may refer to a pending trial or to another defendant. No report connects them.
